after.worked_solution:
First, let's denote 

$\,$ ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 5 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ 

We proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows.

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**: Next, we find ${v}_{2}$, by using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{2}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{(-2)\cdot 1+5\cdot (-2)+3\cdot 2}{{1}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 5 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+\frac{2}{3}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{4}{3} \\ \frac{11}{3} \\ \frac{13}{3}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $B={{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-\frac{4}{3} \\ \frac{11}{3} \\ \frac{13}{3}\end{aligned}]}$ is an orthogonal basis for $V.$

Finally, we have $a=-\frac{4}{3},$ $c=\frac{13}{3},$ and 

$$
\frac{a}{c}=\frac{(-\frac{4}{3})}{(\frac{13}{3})}=-\frac{4}{13}.
$$

We proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows.

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**: Next, we find ${v}_{2}$, by using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{2}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{3\cdot (-1)+(-2)\cdot 5+\sqrt{7}\cdot 0}{(-1)^{2}+{5}^{2}+{0}^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2 \\ \sqrt{7}\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2} \\ \sqrt{7}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

Finally, we have $a=\frac{5}{2},$ $b=\frac{1}{2},$ and 

$$
\frac{b}{a}=\frac{(\frac{1}{2})}{(\frac{5}{2})}=\frac{1}{5}.
$$
